This past weekend, I had the opportunity to compete in the Google DevFest WashU 2025 hackathon! 🚀 Out of 42 teams and 113 hackers from 6 different colleges and universities, my team was selected as one of just 10 finalists! 🎉 Given 24 hours, a Gemini API key, and the theme "AI in ___," we were challenged to build an innovative AI solution for an industry using Google Gemini. Two hours in, we landed on our idea: AI in Software Engineering. With the rise of engineers relying on AI-generated code (or what many now call "vibe coders"), it’s becoming harder to onboard new teammates, pick up where someone else left off, or even just understand existing code. I worked with Sochie Odunlami , Henry Anyimadu , and Koji Wong to build Unveil AI, a full-stack web app that helps engineers (or really anyone) make sense of code. By just uploading a GitHub repo or local directory, you can: • Get line-by-line explanations of your code • Ask clarifying questions about specific files or functions • Even receive a phone call from an AI “senior developer” (powered by Bland AI) who walks you through your codebase Huge shoutout to Isaiah N. Granet for providing us with free Bland AI API tokens, this feature wouldn’t have been possible without him. “Why would we compete with a $14B giant?” “How did Duolingo make hundreds of millions and still get no one fluent?” “Another language app? Isn’t there thousands of those?” Those were my exact questions when my co-founder Erik Dahl told me he wanted to build another language app. At first, I wasn’t convinced. But after working with Erik on a few startups, I knew one thing about him: if he’s obsessed with an idea, it’s probably worth exploring. Then Julia Hudea joined, we met in a university entrepreneurship class at The University of British Columbia . We’d both worked on things that could’ve worked but didn’t matter to us. This one did. Before writing any code, we: 1. Downloaded 52 language learning apps and used every single one for a few hours. 2. Interviewed 65 language learners across Reddit, Discord, and our circles. 3. Found the comprehensible input method, the most research-backed approach to learning a language (listen first, speak later). We built a simple MVP, just a video player with captions, and took it to students. 60% paid for early access. That moment flipped my skepticism into conviction. Fast forward, Parrot is now growing super fast, joined Y Combinator 's Fall 2025 batch, and some learners spending 1hr+ on the app. What started as doubt turned into a mission: to connect people by breaking down language barriers. To make learning a language feel as natural and addictive as scrolling TikTok . ...more ...more

TL;DR Apple just gave us the best marketing campaign we could ask for. activity.title: Roughly 13,700 collections jobs open up in America every year, largely replacing people who quit. Even the large banks I talk to can't hire and hold the collections teams they need. Meanwhile consumer debt just hit $5.15 trillion and delinquency is climbing in nearly every category at once. So more accounts are flowing in, and each one is harder to work. The borrower who's late on a credit card is increasingly late on an auto loan too. And all the time, states keep adding rules and complexity that makes it harder and harder to train new agents to be compliant. The reality is that this just isn't a solvable problem with anything but AI. Cost pressures aren't going to reverse. People aren't going to get cheaper. You can't afford to throw money and bodies at a problem - especially when missing a disclosure could lead to a lawsuit or a call from a state AG's office. The only answer - invest now to ensure that you can use AI to mop up the volume, saving your best human agents to handle the complex conversations where empathy and judgement (and sometimes persuasion) are needed. ...more

Zero out of 22. That's how many leaders from major banks and card issuers picked "protect the brand" as their leadership's headline goal for AI. Brand and consistency got nothing. At a customer experience summit. Then I asked what's blocking them from handing routine servicing conversations to AI. The top answer, 33%, was concern about quality and the customer experience. So the customer experience is the thing standing in the way, and it's the one argument nobody is making internally. It makes sense that cost is the one thing that is most frequently discussed as the benefit of AI in servicing - with AI voice agents now more than capable of handling 70-80% of servicing inquiries completely end-end, there are major savings to be had. But that's not the only benefit. Built properly, AI agents can give comprehensive, highly consistent service, 24/7, with zero wait time. That's a much better experience for the vast majority of interactions than waiting on hold - especially if the end of that hold time is a newly trained human agent, tired after 8 hours of repetitive calls. It also means that for the 20% left over you can deploy your best human agents, empowered to use empathy and judgment to deliver a great experience where customers need help outside of your normal policies or in retention contexts. AI raises the customer experience floor so your best human agents can raise the ceiling. ...more

There are no exceptions to federal consumer financial protection laws for new technologies. An AI voice agent that violates the FDCPA is treated exactly like a human collector who does the same thing. But the biggest thing that consumers actually complain about isn’t aggressive language or calling too often: it’s trying to collect on debts that they don’t think they owe. "Attempts to collect debt not owed" has been the number one debt collection complaint every year since the CFPB started accepting them in 2013. Last year the monthly average jumped 115% over the prior two years. The reality is that in a LOT of those cases, the debt is actually real. But the lender behind their loan trades under a different name, or the store where they took point-of-sale financing has nothing to do with the company now calling them. Some, of course, are just trying to get out of paying. And sometimes they're right. While it’s much rarer today, shady operations sometimes try to collect on a debt that was already sold to someone else; and bad record keeping (especially if a lender shut down or got acquired) can result in collectors going after debt that was already repaid. Either way the collector has to prove it, and collections teams have to put significant resourcing into headcount responding to disputes. And a slow response can turn a confused customer into a complaint. AI agents completely change the economics and speed of handling disputes. They can read the original loan contract and get a formal validation notice out in minutes instead of weeks. And they can patiently explain to someone what they signed and when as many times as they need to hear it. Eventually loans will be tokenized on the blockchain (a longer post…) and disputes should be a thing of the past. Until then, answering "I don't owe this" quickly and kindly is the highest-return compliance work in collections - and one of the best places to implement AI. ...more

A friend who built a billion dollar company told me he thinks every decision is really a gut decision that we rationalize afterwards. When I was younger I'd have found that very surprising. I was relentlessly scientific about everything. I assumed every problem had an irreducible right answer if you just thought about it carefully enough, and I spent years hunting for it. As I got older, I realized that many exceptional people don't work that way at all - they seemingly shoot from the hip, and still hit most of the time. Noah Smith just published an interesting piece on why with AI superintelligence has effectively arrived - but the world looks strangely unchanged. One explanation he explores is that intelligence has an optimality bound: more intelligence less like making a tower taller, and more like making a ball rounder. While there are some things, like coding and math, that have smooth, verifiable solution spaces that enable AI to supersede human ability, this isn't true for most of what matters. We live in a chaotic and unpredictable world; and while we can get to a reasonable assumption of what's going on, at some point the cost of learning more outweighs the benefits. And it's possible that 'human level intelligence' is already pretty much at peak for making educated guesses of what to do in an uncertain and not-completely-knowable problem space. This doesn't mean that rational thinking and a rigorous process doesn't have value. But for complex decisions, a rigorous process has to be input into what is ultimately a gut decision. My general approach to many major decisions was inspired by Daniel Kahneman, in Thinking Fast & Slow, who wrote about how he designed the Israeli army's interview system in the 50s. The original system was a gut call after an unstructured 20 minute interview, which had poor predictive power. He replaced it with six traits, scored one at a time, which took it from useless to moderately useful. Then, to appease the interviewers who hated being turned into robots, he let them close their eyes at the end and give one intuitive score. Interestingly, he found that the gut call *after* going through the rigorous interview process was just as predictive as the whole scoring system. Structure didn't replace intuition - it made intuition work. This is my default mode today. Run a fast but rational process to gather information and assess pros and cons, then make a gut call. Past a certain point, trying to get more information stops buying you accuracy and starts buying you false precision, and can make your decision making worse, not better. Whether you're interviewing a candidate, making a major strategic choice, deciding on which vendor to pick - run a rigorous process, but then trust your gut and go with the vibes. ...more

78% of Gen Z and Millennials say they've received debt collection calls they thought were scams. They do what most of us do now when the phone rings from an unknown number: they ignore it. This is a big challenge for collections teams, especially now that "younger borrowers" hold the majority of delinquent debt. Right-party contact rates are falling across the whole industry, and call screening is spreading fast, both as a habit and as a carrier feature. The answer isn't just to abandon voice - it still converts better than anything else once someone actually picks up, and digital-only strategies don't the same results. So the answer isn't less voice. It's to use it in a smart way as part of a personalized omnichannel strategy. Three things we consistently see work: A good voicemail, because a call back is worth more than a dial. Email and SMS that let a borrower engage on their own terms and drive inbound calls. And a text sent immediately before or after a call attempt, so the number on their screen arrives with context attached. At Veritus our agents work across voice, SMS and email with shared context, sequenced per borrower based on what they actually respond to. And our voice agents handle screening gracefully instead of burning the attempt. Getting picked up is the hardest part of collections now. More dials by themselves won't fix it. ...more

30 petabytes of collider data. That was Jayram Palamadai 's job at CERN, where he worked as a distributed computing engineer getting collider data out to physicists. At that scale you stop thinking about files and start questioning the protocol underneath them, so he designed a different architecture. That became Byteport . It's built on DART, a proprietary transport protocol developed by engineers out of CERN. TCP cuts its congestion window the moment it detects packet loss and then recovers slowly; DART holds near-constant throughput instead, roughly 98 Mbps on a 100 Mbps connection whatever the latency, jitter, or loss. In the field, Byteport has hit speeds up to 1,500× faster than TCP. It runs wherever critical infrastructure runs: on-premises, air-gapped, hybrid, cloud. And in those places a failed transfer isn't a file that shows up late. It's a training run stalled at the data-loading step, a satellite pass that comes and goes, a drone flying without the map it was supposed to have. Byteport runs in all of them. It holds up in intermittent connectivity, high latency, and contested RF. DART runs mission-critical networks spanning land, air, sea, and space. 🎙️ Jayram Palamadai , Founder & CEO, Byteport on Fondo START Full ep: https://fondo.ai/4gs15hq

Every app you've ever used was built for the average user. That's why you have to learn it. At the T-Mobile hackathon, I prototyped the alternative: a version of T-Life where the user journey generates itself around each request instead of being pre-built for everyone. One sentence in: "Upgrade my plan, add 2 lines, and purchase 2 iPhone 17 Pros for them." Today that's a plan comparison screen, two separate line-add flows, two device configurations, and a checkout. Assuming you already know where everything lives. In the prototype, the interface for that exact request generates itself, personalized to your account and populated with real plans and real inventory. You confirm once. It executes. How it works: the backend is exposed to an agent as tools, so the agent can do everything the app can. Three agents split the work. → Planner: sequences every action and identifies what info is still missing from you, pulling live data so the generated UI reflects what's actually available → UI Generation: renders only the interface needed to collect it → Execution: runs the actions and returns confirmation This is personalization at the interface layer. Not a personalized feed inside a fixed app, but an app that assembles itself around the person using it. A week later at Product Day, I heard CTO John Saw describe a vision where T-Life becomes each customer's own personal T-Life. Hearing the company's direction land on the exact problem I'd built for was the best possible confirmation I'd been aiming at the right thing. The hackathon was my shot at asking: what if the fix isn't a better menu, but no fixed menu at all? Demo below 👇

publications.description: We developed and evaluated a fully automated pipeline consisting of two deep learning methods to automate volumetric and regional strain analysis of the RV from contrast-enhanced, ECG-gated cineCT images. The Right Heart Blood Segmenter (RHBS) is a 3D high resolution configuration of nnU-Net to define the endocardial boundary, while the Right Ventricular Wall Labeler (RVWL) is a 3D point cloud-based deep learning method to label the free and septal walls. We trained our models using a diverse cohort of patients with different RV phenotypes and tested in an independent cohort of patients with aortic stenosis undergoing TAVR.

A 49-year-old father lost his voice to a stroke. AI gave it back to him. Not a robotic imitation. His own voice, rebuilt. Last November, James lost his ability to speak. His kids missed his laugh. His wife missed hearing him say her name. Then Bland, an AI voice company, used just 5 seconds of old footage to recreate his voice with its new Speech v3 Human Speech Engine. His tone. His emotion. Even his laugh. The first thing James said was: “I got my voice back.” For business leaders, the significance goes far beyond an impressive AI demo. Voice is becoming the next major interface between people and AI. As speech models become more realistic, they could reshape customer service, healthcare, accessibility and sales. Bland says Speech v3 was trained on more than 100 million real human conversations and ranks 1st on Audio Realism benchmarks. But the benchmark isn’t the most important part. The real opportunity is building AI experiences that don’t just automate communication, but preserve the qualities that make communication feel human. Because as AI becomes more capable, trust, authenticity, and emotional connection may become the real differentiators. As voice AI becomes nearly indistinguishable from human speech, where’s the biggest opportunity to use it without losing the human connection? BREAKING: Bland Speech v3 by Bland debuts as the most human-sounding TTS model on our newest evaluation: Audio Realism Bench. Traditional speech benchmarks increasingly struggle to separate frontier systems that all sound clean, fluent, and intelligible. Audio Realism Bench instead asks a harder question: when two voices read the same transcript, which one sounds more like a real person? Vetted native speakers evaluate recordings blindly across phone agents, conversational assistants, and spoken explainers, judging the subtle qualities that define human-like speech. We also place real human recordings directly into the evaluation pool, testing whether evaluators can distinguish TTS models from actual human speech. Bland Speech v3 takes the top spot in our initial rankings, followed by MAI-Voice-2 by Microsoft AI and Grok TTS by SpaceXAI , all demonstrating important steps toward voice systems capable of sustaining genuinely human-feeling interactions. publications.title: LEGOS-SLEEC: Tool for Formalizing and Analyzing Normative Requirements
publications.subtitle: 2025 International Conference on Software Engineering
publications.description: Systems interacting with humans, such as assistive robots or chatbots, are increasingly integrated into our society. To prevent these systems from causing social, legal, ethical, empathetic, or cultural (SLEEC) harms, normative requirements specify the permissible range of their behaviors. These requirements encompass both functional and non-functional aspects and are defined with respect to time. Typically, these requirements are specified by stakeholders from a broad range of fields, such as lawyers, ethicists, or philosophers, who may lack technical expertise. Because such stakeholders often have different goals, responsibilities, and objectives, ensuring that these requirements are well-formed is crucial. SLEEC DSL, a domain-specific language resembling natural language, has been developed to formalize these requirements as SLEEC rules. In this paper, we present LEGOS-SLEEC, a tool designed to support interdisciplinary stakeholders in specifying normative requirements as SLEEC rules, and in analyzing and debugging their well-formedness. LEGOS-SLEEC is built using four previously published components, which have been shown to be effective and usable across nine case studies. Reflecting on this experience, we have significantly improved the user interface of LEGOS-SLEEC and its diagnostic support, and demonstrate the effectiveness of these improvements using four interdisciplinary stakeholders

publications.description: This paper introduces a novel approach to reducing systematic uncertainties in LArTPC detector simulations, which arise from known detector effects that are challenging and computationally intensive to model. activity.title: Summit won audience choice at TroyLabs pitch night 🏔️🏔️ I keep thinking about how unlikely that sentence sounded a semester ago. I first met my co-founders Lucas Rival and Joseph Choi at USC's incubator LavaLab , where we spent nine weeks getting humbled. We pivoted more than any other team in the cohort. We found the idea for Summit after I tried to find my dad's business by asking ChatGPT for the best contractors. His story and his company weren't showing up in the fastest growing sales platform. We came back from spring break with two weeks left before demo day, and our pitch was so scrappy that we were almost blocked from the stage. The number of late nights and Red Bulls we went through... but it worked. We pitched, landed our first paying customer, and left LavaLab with something real. The following semester we got into Troylabs, USC's premier startup accelerator. The accelerator was a different game. We grew the team, got more chances to pitch in front of people who write actual checks, and Summit started feeling less like a project and more like a company. A huge part of that was the cracked TroyLabs people who joined us: Jennifer Zhang , Mihika Deshmukh, Matthew Wong , Carter Davis , Melanie Lee , Bryan Ramirez-Gonzalez , Maia Rocha , Dilen Kakar , and Mandy Guo . Nine people who bet on the future of marketing and made it real. Then pitch night came, and we walked away with the win. The check that came with it was technically the first money Summit has ever raised. We're now at 10x the monthly revenue we left LavaLab with. Our habit of pivoting never stopped, so we are still shipping new features. Couldn't have asked for better co-founders, teammates, and mentors!

Spent the last few days at ICLR 2026 in Rio 🇧🇷 We asked: when different LLMs learn the same task, do they solve it the same way internally? Spoiler: no. Qwen models use tight, localized circuits. Llama and Gemma distribute the same computation across way more components. The deeper takeaway: we're building increasingly powerful systems and still barely know what's happening inside them. Mech interp is one of the more honest attempts to fix that. Grateful to my co-authors Arya Bhardia , Julian Ramirez , and Syd Verma ! Paper: https://lnkd.in/ggKqPWKS see y'all at ACL 👋

Make the most of your college friends, because you might be stuck with them for a while. At least, that’s what the brilliant Steve Johnson (Head of design @ Netflix ) told us today during his unforgettable visit to LavaLab . But taking advantage of college years wasn’t the only wisdom that Steve shared as he dutifully answered a barrage of questions. Here are my top 3 takeaways: 1. Storytelling is your delta. When asked about how to stand out in today’s market, it wasn't any hard skill, but persuasion. If you can clearly articulate your vision and captivate an audience, you become invincible. This is what distinguishes great leaders and designers in today's market. Don't just do the work -- sell the vision. 2. Risky business is good business. Impactful achievements are made through bold action, not repeating old successes. You need to adopt a risk mindset and be willing to fail early and often, especially during your college years. It's cheesy but true: if you want a shot at breaking through the noise — both as a person and a company — you have to put something on the line. 3. Birds of a feather stick together. Steve described how throughout his career he has surrounded himself with the same friends and co-workers that drive success in every role. You will probably meet you lifelong co-workers and co-founders in college, if not right after. The most valuable thing you gain from college is the people you meet, so never stop meeting people. At Lavalab we share the very same belief in the importance of finding your co-founders in college. We couldn't be more thankful for your time and wisdom today, Steve Johnson !

This summer, I had the incredible opportunity to participate in NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration ’s Student Airborne Research Program (SARP)! Over the course of the program, I flew aboard several NASA research aircraft, including the Langley G-III equipped with GCAS and AWP, the Langley G-V with HSRL-2, and the Armstrong G-III with UAVSAR. Seeing these instruments operate in the field was one of the highlights of the summer. I also participated in fieldwork around Galveston Bay, collecting data with the University of Houston’s mobile air quality laboratory and research vessel and launching weather balloons equipped with radiosondes and ozonesondes. Another highlight was working with some of my peers to prepare and deliver a weather forecast briefing for SARP flight operations. This gave me a firsthand look at how meteorology, instrumentation, and mission planning come together during an airborne campaign. For my research project, I used airborne LiDAR observations from AWP and HALO to investigate mountain wave signatures in the atmosphere. This project introduced me to atmospheric dynamics from a remote sensing perspective and made me especially excited about the potential of airborne LiDAR to observe processes that may be difficult to fully resolve using models or satellites alone! SARP was incredibly impactful in helping me clarify the direction I hope to take in Earth science and remote sensing, but more than anything, I am grateful to my mentors, program staff, and everyone in SARP East and West who made this experience so meaningful. A special shout-out to my Atmosphere East group: Hannah Akel , Zayna Haider , Samantha (Sammy) Lee , Matthew Simpson , and Kiaya McCuin! Thank you to my faculty mentors, Mary Angelique G. Demetillo and Dan Goldberg , my graduate mentor, Leo Bloxham , and the AWP and HALO PIs, Kristopher Bedka and Amin Nehrir , for their guidance and support throughout my project. Finally, thank you to Cynthia Hall , Yaítza Luna-Cruz, Ph.D., Joelle Hopkins , ECR, and everyone who supported the program. I am incredibly thankful for this summer and so excited to carry these experiences forward!

A strange thing happens to many high-achieving students. At some point they stop studying the subject...and then start studying themselves. A strange shift happens. Chemistry, calculus, literature, and math slowly stop being the source of stress. The student's relationship with themselves becomes the real battlefield. Too many questions nagging at students, with a constant roaring of inner voices such as how much have I finished?how much has she finished? Am I behind or why am I tired already? and some of them become harsher, becoming self- accusatory ..Shouldn't I be working harder? What if everyone else is handling this better than I am? After years of working with IB and AP students, I've noticed something interesting. The students who struggle the most are not always the ones with the hardest courses nor with the weakest foundations.. Sometimes they're the students who spend the entire day watching themselves learn, constantly evaluating, measuring, second-guessing themselves. After delving into neuroscience, I now understand better. The brain doesn't really distinguish between solving a problem and worrying about the problem. In fact, both consume mental resources. This means while a student is trying to learn electrochemistry, part of their attention is busy asking "am I behind?" same for Literature too. While they're reading Shakespeare, another part is wondering, what score will this get me? At some point, the subject is no longer the main workload but self-monitoring is. Here is the problem - this kind of exhaustion is particularly cruel because it looks like laziness from the outside. Perhaps with a student sitting at the desk, books open, ipad is on but t half of their energy is being spent managing anxiety rather than learning. One of the most helpful things(hopefully) I tell my students during exam season is that they don't need to monitor yourself every minute to be a responsible student. Nor do they need to constantly calculate their worth through productivity. Perhaps the most productive thing a student can do is stop asking whether they do "enough" and return to the next page. The next question. that next small step. Because learning requires attention. unfortunately, attention is expensive. Meaning? the more of it we spend watching ourselves, the less of it remains for the thing we are actually trying to learn. ...more ...more

💡 Proteins aren't static – they constantly shift between different shapes, and those motions are often essential to their function. Yet, many AI structure prediction models collapse this complexity into a single "best" structure. We are excited to share a new study, co-authored by Eric and Wendy Schmidt Center postdoctoral fellow Sanketh Vedula , which addresses this long-standing challenge. Published in Nature Biotechnology, this work introduces experiment-guided AlphaFold3, a framework that integrates experimental data from techniques such as NMR, X-ray crystallography, and cryo-EM into AlphaFold3 to reconstruct ensembles of protein structures that better reflect biological reality. By capturing structural heterogeneity rather than a single conformation, the approach opens new possibilities for studying protein dynamics, advancing inverse protein design, and accelerating drug discovery. Congratulations to Sanketh, and co-authors Advaith Sai , Nadav Bojan Sellam , Meital Bojan , Volodymyr Masalitin , Paul Schanda , Ailie Marx , and Alex Bronstein on this exciting milestone, and to collaborators at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA), TEL HAI Academic College , MIGAL Galilee Research Institute , Princeton University , and the Schmidt Center at the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard . The team’s follow-up study is going to be presented at #ICML2026 , which introduces a general inference-time optimization framework that addresses limitations in the reverse‑diffusion process, and results in consistently more accurate experiment-grounded ensembles. #ProteinStructure #AlphaFold #StructuralBiology #AIinBiology #MachineLearning Nature Portfolio ...more ...more

Screw vibe coding. Take matters into your own hands. Every AI model you use is bloated and inefficient. They need trillions of 16 bit weights when only 2 bits can do. That’s why I built my own 2-bit language model by hand. Introducing Avenue, a family of ternary language models that can train on your MacBook. Named after the avenues of East Village, NYC. The best 2-bit model performs better than a full precision model 25% bigger than itself. At scale, a model that needs 8GB would fit in 1GB. All trained on a MacBook Pro in 43 hours. And the best part, I wrote every single line of code by hand, not via an AI agent. That includes a custom tokenizer, a training pipeline with Quantization-aware training (QAT) support, and an inference stack with Post-training Quantization (PTQ) ability. The sample generation below speaks for itself. We see that FP and QAT ternary are close, while PTQ sucks. Doing this was hard. So I’m making it easier for others: I wrote a ~1900 word math explainer on how 2-bit models actually work, everything is open source, and the models are up on HuggingFace. Links in comments. Next step: MLX and a GPT-2 scale model.

OpenRelay (YC S26) provides one API for inference across every chip. OpenRelay gives developers a single entry point for inference across every accelerator. You send a workload; OpenRelay schedules it onto the best-fit chip - NVIDIA, AMD, Trainium, or TPU - across clouds and hands back one production endpoint, typically 20% cheaper than renting the hardware yourself. You never pick the chip, chase quotas, or rebuild your stack per provider. It works in both directions: operators with idle accelerators can connect capacity to OpenRelay’s rails and get inference demand without building a platform themselves. The company is live in production, running 100 billion tokens a week across 22 locations on four continents and 11 accelerator SKUs. Jaden Wang built a half-megawatt data center and built virtualization at Voltage Park. Prashant Patel developed accelerator infrastructure at AWS, writing custom kernels for Trainium. They saw the same gap from opposite sides: there’s more AI compute than ever, and you still can’t reach it. Congrats on the launch, Jaden and Prashant! 🚀 https://lnkd.in/gSAqpV6U

projects.title: STRIDE: Stroke Kinetic Therapy System
projects.description: STRIDE is a low-cost, automated lower-limb rehabilitation device designed for post-stroke patients in Singapore. The device simultaneously supports knee flexion-extension (0-110 degrees) via a motorised ball-screw actuator and hip abduction-adduction (30 degrees abduction, 10-15 degrees adduction) via a curved rail mechanism, making it the first device at its price point to address both joints together.Built for SGD 807 in verified materials, STRIDE is 2.7x cheaper than the nearest comparable commercial CPM machine and over 60x cheaper than robotic exoskeletons. The device is designed to fit within a standard Singapore HDB flat and be used safely without a clinician present.A cloud-connected monitoring layer built on an ESP32 microcontroller and Supabase backend enables real-time caregiver oversight through a Base44 mobile application and Firebase web dashboard. An event-triggered vibration sensor detects and alerts caregivers to sudden patient movements or spasms automatically.As Mechanical Lead and overall team lead, I designed the reverse-V knee linkage, selected and sized the curved rail for anatomically correct hip motion, derived all component dimensions from Singaporean anthropometric data, and led volunteer user trials through multiple rounds of physical testing. I also coordinated integration across the mechanical, electronics, enclosure, and software subsystems.The project was presented at the Industrial Transformation Asia-Pacific (ITAP) 2025 Conference on 16 October 2025 to Mr. Alvin Tan, Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry. The project received a formal written endorsement from industry partner Clemvision, was showcased at NUS CDE Day 2025, and has been submitted to the Tan Kah Kee Young Inventors' Award 2026, the James Dyson Award 2026, and the NUS CDE Innovation and Research Award 2026.

activity.title: Most Robots built to serve people still feel like black boxes. We wanted to change that. I had one big question coming in as Co-Director of Tech and PM for project Glyph: how can you make a robot more readable to the people it actually interacts with? Our answer: run fluid simulations on the black box. Glyph is a drink-dispensing robot dog equipped with an IMU + LED matrix running real-time fluid dynamics to make the interaction feel more natural. Users can see “liquid” sloshing around as the robot moves and the fluid level decreases as more drinks are dispensed. These goals of improving human-robot interaction have shaped what Terra Labs built for demo this semester: - An end-to-end mobile ordering, autonomous navigation, and drink dispensing system with 3 soda flavors through Glyph - A 7DOF robotic arm serving matcha with an electromagnet end-effector - A projection mapping experience acting as the portal between digital art & people through live hand + face tracking Our club didn’t even exist a semester ago. Because of ~20 cracked engineers + designers, more than 100 people popped out to our showcase. So much love to the talented glyph team: Pan Pitpreecha , Shaurya Goel , Iris Liu Ye , Ellie Lin-Stevens , and Sydney Padilla , it's been so amazing being able to support all of you throughout this past semester. This summer, I’ve had the chance to see a few very different sides of what it means to build with AI and emerging technology. One of those experiences was PwC ’s inaugural Engineer Your Career program in Seattle. Over four days, I learned from PwC engineers and leaders, visited Microsoft’s campus, and worked with a team through a fast paced immersion challenge based on a real world corporate crisis. Our scenario involved a large scale game developer facing growing customer frustration during a major campaign. Its automated support system could resolve simple tickets, but the company still struggled to respond quickly when issues became more complex and crossed multiple teams. Our team designed a system that gave operations teams direct visibility into the campaign and routed each issue to the right owner. Building the tech was only part of it. The harder part was figuring out how it would actually be introduced, whether teams would adopt it, and whether it could hold up as the company scaled. A tool can be technically impressive and still fail if it doesn’t fit the people, systems, and workflows it has to live within. A huge thank you to PwC for bringing together engineers, students, and builders from across the country, each with a different lens on the same messy problem, and giving us the chance to work through these challenges firsthand. Thank you as well to Fayez Ahmed and Ivan Vinogradov for leading our team and sharing so much about their work and experiences. Novel perspectives, and the chance to keep learning from other builders, is a big part of why I’m extremely excited to attend YC Startup School this week! At Engineer Your Career, I got to see what it takes to apply new technology inside large, complex organizations. At Startup School, I’m excited to explore the other side of that process: how builders identify the right problems, work through uncertainty, and turn early ideas into products and systems that people adopt. For the past several months I've been building something I wanted for myself: a place to learn robotics, meet other people building in the space, and share what I'm learning along the way - a real community of learners and roboticists. It's called Leet Robotics, and it's live today. The idea is simple. Courses and learning content, completely free. this might be the best week in tech so far this year. Fable 5 got extended until July 17th. OpenAI also released the GPT-5.6 family. both are amazing on their own. together, they’re one of the greatest tools a builder can have right now. Fable 5 is still the best model I’ve used for architecture, planning, understanding tradeoffs, and figuring out how a large task should actually be approached. the issue is the usage limits. even on Anthropic’s 20x Max plan, it’s extremely easy to burn through your subscription. so I built a setup that lets Fable stay in charge while delegating most of the work to the GPT-5.6 family. here’s how I use them: -> Sol is OpenAI’s strongest reasoning model. great for long tasks and complex implementation. it will get it done. -> Terra is a solid middle-ground worker. good for tasks that need more than a basic model without using Sol. -> Luna is dirt cheap and ideal for simple work like searching files, gathering context, or small tasks. Fable handles the architecture, planning, delegation, and final review. the GPT-5.6 models handle the execution. Fable can even delegate tasks that use OpenAI’s computer-use capabilities, which is still by far the best way I’ve found to give an agent real access to your computer. this means it can gather context, refactor large sections of a codebase, investigate issues, implement changes, test the work, and send agents back in when something is still broken. a task that would previously burn through my weekly Fable usage within 30 minutes now uses around 5% of my 5 hour limit. Fable gets to focus on what it’s best at instead of wasting its limited usage on every small implementation step. the GPT-5.6 models get a much smarter system planning and reviewing their work. I’ve been using this for long coding tasks, large refactors, parallel issue fixing, context gathering, and everything in between. comment “foreman” and I’ll send you the repo. #buildinpublic #ai #codex #claudecode #codingagents

a forecast I read is the reason I'm in SF right now A few summers ago I was messing around on Replit, watching random AI videos, and stumbled across a deep dive on AI 2027. read it and couldn't stop. it showed me we're in the middle of one of the biggest technological shifts in history, and that's what sent me down the path that eventually landed me in SF. Seeing GPT-5.6 move through a limited rollout at the government's request, and Fable/Mythos access get suspended after national-security concerns reminded me of AI 2027 (a forecast about frontier AI, arms races, and loss of control). a lot of people are framing this as government overreach or labs losing momentum. I understand that concern, but I don't think that's the only way to see it. AI 2027 is essentially about what happens when every lab and every government races forward because standing still feels like losing. building blindly. shipping fast. treating caution as weakness. what we're seeing now, phased releases, safety evaluations, more outside review before broad public access, might be the start of something healthier. I'm not saying blanket bans or permanent gatekeeping are the answer. but given how uncertain things are at the frontier, slowing down slightly and being more deliberate seems reasonable. I'm curious if this turns into something consistent and transparent with real standards, or if it stays reactive. one is progress. other is politics dressed up as safety. Link in the comments. Check out AI 2027 if you haven't, genuinely one of the most important things I've come across.

Today marked one of our favorite milestones of the year: Celebrating Science, our end-of-summer poster session, where RockEDU students shared the research they have spent months building alongside their mentors with our scientific community, friends, and families. Each poster was a snapshot of student research. But each poster also represented far more than a science project. It reflected weeks of curiosity, persistence, collaboration, problem-solving, and mentorship. It was a celebration of scientific discovery, and of the people and relationships that make discovery possible. This year's event brought together students from across several RockEDU pathways: ** RockEDU Undergraduate Research Scholars (RURS), which places students who complete our CURE into year-long paid research internships at Rockefeller (a program led by Jessi Hersh, PhD ) ** SSRP In Situ, led by Doug Heigl, which gives SSRP alumni the opportunity to return to Rockefeller for immersive summer research experiences in campus laboratories. ** And, of course, our longstanding Summer Science Research Program (SSRP), whose students spent the summer asking meaningful questions, learning new techniques, and contributing to research alongside outstanding scientist mentors. An event like this is the result of extraordinary care from an incredible team. Jen Bohn worked tirelessly to prepare and support our mentors, ensuring they had the tools and confidence to guide students through an authentic research experience. Jessi Hersh once again made sure every student felt supported from beginning to end, creating an environment where they could do their best work and confidently share it with others. To our RockEDU Fellows, scientist mentors, teaching teams, laboratory hosts, and support staff: thank you. The culture of learning you create is every bit as important as the science itself. We were also delighted to welcome Dannielle Kenny from Cape Town, South Africa, who spent time shadowing the SSRP as she explored ideas to bring back to her own institution. One of the greatest compliments we can receive is seeing others invest in adapting and growing these models within their own communities. We look forward to seeing where those ideas lead. Over the years, this celebration has grown into an ecosystem built through partnerships across Rockefeller and throughout New York City, where multiple entry points, sustained mentorship, and authentic research experiences help students continue to see themselves as scientists. It is exciting to see that ecosystem beginning to inspire conversations well beyond our own campus. We are incredibly proud of what our students accomplished this summer, and even more proud of the community they built together. Onward!

The View from the Office. I met up with Kaelan Yim , a rising junior studying computer science at the University of California, Berkeley, at the Bryant Park Cafe. He had quesadillas; I had the sliders. Kaelan grew up in the Bay Area. While neither of his parents worked in tech, he became interested in computer programming because of a passion for video games. He estimates he played about five hours of Minecraft a day in high school. He arrived at Berkeley planning after graduation to work on computer chip manufacturing. But friends steered his interest in the direction of AI safety research. He got a chance to work on benchmarks and evals for frontier models as a Cambridge MARS scholar and this summer he is visiting Washington for a policy program run by the Hertog Foundation with the Institute for the Study of War. One of the fun things about connecting with someone so much younger is the perspective they provide. Our conversation ranged from the percentage of Berkley students using AI to cheat on tests (high) to the red-pilled San Francisco AI culture. We covered a lot of ground, including his sense of the difference between fellowships like Z Fellows and those arranged by Thiel and the 776 Foundation as well as the evolution of Y Combinator and the recent debate over closed and open-sourced AI model builders. On the side, Kaelan does robotics research. He managed to procure a lidar sensor similar to the kind Waymo mounts on its vehicles and he’s using it to train robots recorded from a third-person perspective. He said the best thing about attending Berkeley isn’t the classes so much as the community. In education, the fundamentals still matter because you need to know the basics to understand the tech. Kaelan is a proponent of open weight models and he expects the enormous price differentials between US models from companies like Anthropic and the Chinese models like Kimi K3. He has a wide range of hobbies beyond AI including spelunking, leatherworking, glassblowing, crochet, gardening, autocross, cinema and axe throwing. He told me there are four things he wants to see during his lifespan: humans living beyond Earth, autonomous robots, fusion power, and research into human cognition. You can connect with Kaelan via LinkedIn or X or DM me for a warm intro.

Every year, over 1,000,000 people are injured at intersections. The warning signs are almost always there first, but they're buried in 311 tickets, Nextdoor threads, social media posts, and local news — too scattered for anyone to act on. This past weekend, my team built something to pull those signals together. It won Best Use of Claude at UC Berkeley's AI Hackathon. 🏆 Meet SafeStreets, an AI web app that unifies these sources into ready-to-send advocacy reports. Here's how it works: → See it: Orchestrated parallel bots that gather complaints, local news, and government records (via Browserbase and public APIs), while Claude Vision reads street and satellite imagery to spot the hazards. → Corroborate it. Everything flows into a shared Redis memory layer, where Claude cross-references and votes across sources to confirm a real case — then distills it into a structured spec. → Act on it. Gemini Nano Banana 2 renders before-and-after fixes, and Claude-orchestrated agents draft the Reddit posts, tweets, and the emails to your local council rep. The problem: you give your engineering team AWS Bedrock access. Productivity jumps. So does your bill: fast, unpredictable, and impossible to break down. When finance asks "who spent what, on which project, using which model?", nobody can answer. The usual reflex is a proxy or a wrapper in front of Bedrock, which becomes a bottleneck, a single point of failure, and one more thing to operate. The solution: govern at the AWS layer itself, so there's nothing in the request path to break or bypass. • Works with the coding agents your developers already use. Claude Code, Kiro CLI, and OpenAI Codex CLI each ship governance hooks that give early warnings before a call is ever made. Because enforcement lives in AWS, not the client, the same rules hold no matter which tool a developer runs, and adding a new one is just another set of hooks. • Service Control Policies gate model access org-wide. Opus stays denied until access is approved. A developer can edit their config, pass --model opus, or write raw boto3, and AWS still rejects the call at the API boundary. It's not a client setting to misconfigure around. • IAM principal tags flow into CUR 2.0, so every Bedrock call is attributed to a project, team, and cost center automatically. No headers, no environment variables, no developer effort. The attribution is structural, and it shows up in Cost Explorer and Athena. • Token budgets keep usage efficient without friction. Per-developer budgets run in advisory mode by default: developers get early-warning signals as they approach a threshold and self-correct, with no throttling or blocked calls in the way of their work. Turn on hard enforcement only where you need it. • A Step Functions approval workflow turns premium-model access into a self-service request instead of a ticket queue. • No proxy, no wrapper, no gateway. The governance lives in Organizations, IAM, and CUR: services you already run. The one-sentence version: developers get fast AI access, finance gets a predictable and fully attributed bill, and neither depends on anyone remembering to follow the rules. VCU NSF REU Site Students Showcase Digital Forensics Research at the 26th Annual DFRWS USA Conference—and Earn a Poster Award I am pleased to share that students from the Virginia Commonwealth University NSF Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU) Site in Digital Forensics attended the 26th Annual Digital Forensics Research Conference (DFRWS USA 2026) in Arlington, Virginia, hosted by George Mason University . The REU students presented posters highlighting the research they conducted during the summer program. The participating students represented institutions across the country: Logan Altomonte — James Madison University Arya Kunisetty — University of California, Los Angeles Sasha Babic — Randolph-Macon College Cosme Boisset — Louisiana State University New Orleans Sebastian Alcibar — Virginia Commonwealth University Emirhan Kir — Rowan University Zoe McIvor — Longwood University Vaishnavi Sharma — Purdue University Sanskriti Gyawali — Virginia Commonwealth University Their projects addressed a broad range of timely digital-forensics and cybersecurity challenges, including PLC security, unmanned aerial systems, point-of-care ultrasound forensics, Starlink network behavior, passive Wi-Fi sensing, cybercrime against older adults, and explainable AI-assisted authorship analysis. Special congratulations to Arya Kunisetty , whose poster, “Forensic Attribution of Human and Autonomous Control in Unmanned Aerial Systems,” received third prize in the poster competition. His work explored whether recovered drone telemetry can distinguish autonomous flight from human control and support the forensic attribution of individual pilots. We also sincerely thank Arya’s mentors, Suramya Pokharel and Eyuphan Bulut , for their guidance, technical support, and commitment to his research. This recognition reflects Arya’s hard work as well as the valuable mentorship that helped shape the project. Congratulations to all the REU students for their hard work, professionalism, and excellent presentations. I am deeply grateful to the faculty members, postdoctoral researchers, graduate-student mentors, and collaborators who helped the students develop their research ideas, conduct rigorous experiments, prepare their posters, and confidently present their work. I am also grateful to Dr. Kemal Akkaya , Chair of the Department of Computer Science, and the VCU College of Engineering administration, including Dean Azim Eskandarian , Senior Associate Dean Gary Tepper , and Associate Dean for Research and Innovation Susan Barker , for their continued support of undergraduate research, faculty mentorship, and the NSF REU program. I'm two weeks off of Spring Quarter at UCI, and I wish I could say I was relaxing! These past two weeks I've been spending my days in my internship at LoopNet , learning in the ins and outs of industry-standard software development, and in my nights to the early morning, I've been grinding out the production of my student team's game Dungeon Dilemma leading us to our release today! First, work at LoopNet has been a whirlwind! While I knew that my college courses only covered the basics, I didn't know that they were "that" basic in comparison to real development. I've absolutely loved my time with my team so far, and I'm super eager to learn more from the developers on my team and the workshops offered every week. Although I'm definitely not understanding everything I hear in standups everyday, it has been so fun hearing about new features being planned, worked on, and shipped for a REAL product (I like meetings, what can I say?). Speaking of learning, my experience leading and working on Dungeon Dilemma was all about breaking through those fears of the unknown and failing. My team and I had never worked on multiplayer before, but we decided to take the plunge last Spring and stuck with it through vacations, refactors, and so many sleep-depriving bugs. Wrapping my head around production flows was also its own challenge - managing so many different students' and my own schedules, and I'm actually so proud that my team and I fought through the fires of learning and landed on such a polished final product, featuring in Steam Next Fest last week, releasing on Steam ( https://lnkd.in/gX-6QkbN ) today, and showing at numerous showcases including the SGDA Summit this weekend! Lining up two weeks at LoopNet and the release of my team's game was definitely not my intention, but it's been fun to reflect on how the two, a platform for commercial real estate and a rag-tag group of amateur student game developers, cross over. Both are extremely end-user focused. Both need rigorous collaboration across teams and departments. Both require me to step outside of my comfort zone. Both have me wondering, "What is going on???" every work session. Would I recommend myself to do it again? No. Sleeping at 4 AM on a Friday is probably not the best idea. Will I listen to that advice? Nope! I still have so much more to learn!

publications.description: My reflective essay “Commanding a Millennium Odyssey” appears in Elevate Magazine — Issue 4 “Journey,” published by Boston University’s Newbury Center for first-generation students (2025). In the piece, I trace my leap from home to college through the image of a fiery-orange sunset seen from an airplane window, wrestling with what it means to leave family, carry multiple identities, and redefine “success” beyond grades or titles. The story invites readers to embrace uncertainty, honor their roots, and craft a personal “story-truth” out of everyday moments of growth. Grateful to add my voice to the first-gen narrative and to keep turning dreams into goals on this continuing odyssey.

projects.title: Sapling
projects.description: Online interactive learning platform that turns every conversation into a structured knowledge map based on degrees of mastery, both academic and personal. Rather than requiring students to manually log their study material, Gemini automatically identifies and tracks concepts in real time, building a live graph of mastery as the session unfolds. The AI model establishes reinforced learning through relevant questioning and custom quizzes, rather than providing an immediate answer. Deadlines and assignments are tracked automatically with calendar authentication from uploaded syllabi and online assignment pages. A social comparison layer lets users view their knowledge tree alongside classmates, online members, or anyone at their school, enabling peer matching based on where each student's understanding diverges and active recall. Built with Next.js, FastAPI, D3.js, Supabase, and Google Gemini.

projects.title: Room Temperature Monitor (EK 131)
projects.description: The design report presents a portable, battery-powered room-temperature monitor that displays the current temperature on a 16 × 2 LCD screen and warns the user with a flashing red LED and piezo buzzer whenever the reading drifts outside a user-defined comfort band (e.g., 70 °F – 80 °F). This goal drives the entire engineering cycle documented in the report, from component selection through testing. At the heart of the prototype is an Arduino Uno, which reads an LM35 analog temperature sensor, drives the I²C LCD, and controls the alert system of LEDs and buzzer. All components are housed in a custom ABS enclosure; a neatly soldered harness collects common ground and 5 V rails, and jumpers route signals to the Arduino headers. Careful LED-current calculations (≈ 3 mA for the green power LED and ≈ 13 mA for the red alarm LED) balance brightness against battery life. Powered by a 9 V, 500 mAh battery regulated down to 5 V, the whole system draws about 70 mA, allowing roughly seven hours of continuous operation before the battery must be replaced or recharged.In operation, the sketch repeatedly samples the LM35, converts the voltage to degrees Fahrenheit, updates the display, and decides whether to trigger the audible-visual alarm. The sensor’s usable range spans –40 °F to 257 °F, and in the prototype the alarm band is set to 80 °F – 90 °F; the buzzer and LED activate immediately when readings leave this band and silence automatically when temperatures return to safe limits. Bench tests with a warm hand and a distant hair-dryer confirmed accurate readings and fast alarms, meeting all primary objectives, though the team notes battery life, weight, and enclosure size as areas for future refinement. Suggested improvements include swapping the Uno for a smaller Arduino Nano, adopting a higher-capacity Li-ion pack or external power supply, and streamlining the housing for better portability.

I was CREATIVELY inspired by Jocelyn V. ’s article on why she paid to return to ColorStack ’s Stacked Up Summit to put together my own breakdown, as someone who was there for the first time. I flew into San Francisco 8 months after joining ColorStack, only 3 months after becoming a member. Not only did feedback like hers, and countless others, shape how I prepared, but this summit turned out to be one of the greatest experiences of my time in ColorStack so far. I didn't wait to be ready, but that didn't mean I felt prepared, only that I wasn't willing to wait. I want to thank Viviana Ayala , my chapter's former and founding president, who not only introduced me to ColorStack but gave me just enough support to do it on my own. I also want to thank the people who made this weekend what it was. Keiyana Arnold, MSOM opened the day with energy (A LOT OF IT!) that carried the whole room. Then Arnell Calderon and Jehron W. Petty , president and CEO, took the stage, and that's when I realized the stranger from the bathroom was the CEO… Trust me, no one felt sillier than I did. Jeffrey Malcolm and Kay Malcolm followed with humor and raw meaning that stayed with me since (Kay Malcolm's line stuck with me the entire weekend: great work matters, so does visibility…). Equally impactful was the fireside chat with Dr. Miguel Angel Hernandez , Teresa Tyson , and Dr. Durryle Brooks, Ph.D, MA that made me think about my own experiences in the workplace. Some things didn't go as planned, but that ended up giving me more motivation. One of my favorite moments were with Ben-James (BJ) Brown who walked us through his path to Wells Fargo . What stood out was how much he loved what he did, and how much he wanted us to know it. I would like to thank once again Jocelyn Vazquez but also Jose Cruz-Lopez for their Campus to Career extensive resources, Arnell Calderon ’s networking tips, the ColorStack Slack community, and the people who made time to create and share their experience in the Level Up Series on YouTube that gave me the frameworks I built my whole approach around. Oh and also(!) the many people who I got to connect with during my weekend in San Francisco! 🌁 A huge thank you to ColorStack for building a community like this, and to Last Mile Education Fund for the support that made this experience possible.

The next capstone we'd like to highlight just wrapped, this one with the University of California, Berkeley LIKELION US student club. Hanjo Kim , Ju Ho Kim , Irene Lee, Chaeeun (Clara) Kim , Jennifer Choi , and Brandon Yea built AURA, an AI co-scientist for innovation research. Thank you to all of you for an exceptional run of work. The question behind the project. Most AI research tools are good at telling you what's known, but innovation teams need something different. They need ranked, defensible bets they can fund, kill, or pivot on. A literature review tells you what is known. A bet tells you what to do next. AURA adapts Google DeepMind's co-scientist architecture into a six-agent loop with Generation, Reflection, Tournament, Evolution, Meta-Review, and a Final Report synthesizer. It borrows Andrej Karpathy's autoresearch ratchet so each round preserves the strongest hypotheses and uses them as the floor for the next. And it adds the piece that's fully theirs, a DomainProfile layer that injects domain-specific scoring weights, seed questions, and source priorities into every agent at runtime. The same six-agent loop produces materially different bets for an eVTOL question versus a robotaxi question. What makes this work stand out isn't just the architecture. It's the engineering honesty. The team shipped a working system and then wrote openly about what's still half-built. A ratchet metric that inherits stale Elo ratings across rounds. An analytics table defined but not yet wired up. Sliders that took two coupled non-linearities to actually respond to user input. That kind of clarity is rare and exactly what makes research reproducible. This matters for research. Most AI research assistants stop at synthesis. The interesting frontier is systems that force a choice, surface the evidence on both sides, and let humans commit a budget with eyes open. AURA is a real step in that direction. Incredible work from this team. The full write-up is in their blog: https://lnkd.in/eadDRjU6

Want to know how to become a great lecturer? Think about the classes you hated. Mine at Berkeley: assignments that never got started in lecture. Professors blasting information while half the room played 2048. Dense slides, heavy load, zero breathing room. So I did the opposite, and the professor loved it. Last week — UC Irvine School of Pharmacy & Pharmaceutical Sciences , PHMD 204B with Professor Gha-hyun Jeffrey Kim, PharmD, PhD . 60 PharmD students. The STRENGTH trial (Omega-3 CA vs. Corn Oil, JAMA 2020). Most of them hadn't read a paper this dense before. That's where Liner Scholar's mission actually lives — not handing you the answer, but lightening the hard parts, deepening understanding, and catching the details a person would easily miss. We used it to surface what the abstract hides: - The early stoppage for futility - The buried atrial fibrillation safety signal - The inclusion criteria most students skim past The students weren't asking whether to use AI. They were asking how to use it without losing the judgment that makes them good clinicians. AI lectures are quietly making their way into high academia. Not as a shortcut. As a safety net. If you teach and want a research AI tool seminar for your students — DM me. Happy to come to you. Zot! Zot! Zot!
